source.title_on_document: Can ChatGPT enhance business student creativity? Evidence from a randomised controlled trial

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix.
supplement.holds: Nothing. All statistics are in the main text and Tables 1 and 2 (PDF p. 9-10). The tables give no per-arm n and do not label the values in parentheses.

paper_design_summary: First-year business undergraduates in 26 classes (Entrepreneurship, Marketing, Management) were randomly assigned within discipline to a 15-minute in-class ideation task with ChatGPT-3.5 or without generative AI (usual resources, including internet search). Entrepreneurship and Marketing students listed uses for a paperclip; Management students generated ideas to return employees to the workplace. Three raters scored fluency (idea count), flexibility, originality, and elaboration; flexibility was dropped before analysis, and the other three were analyzed with MANOVA by discipline.

participants.exclusions: 656 is the sum of the stated discipline counts at recruitment and assignment (Entrepreneurship n = 160, Marketing n = 496). The paper removed duplicates (students attending two subjects), submissions with incomplete data, submissions from students who did not consent, univariate outliers (number not stated), and two multivariate outliers (Mahalanobis). No analyzed N is stated. The reported degrees of freedom (Pillai F(3, 196); univariate F(1, 198)) imply far fewer analyzed students than 656 (about 202 by screener arithmetic, not stated in the paper).

eligibility.reason: Students were individually randomized within discipline to ChatGPT-3.5 or no generative AI, and raters scored fluency, originality, and elaboration on the ideas produced (with AI available). The paper states 1190 participants (656 in S1, 534 in S2) at recruitment and assignment but never states the analyzed N; the degrees of freedom imply roughly 200 (S1) and 120 (S2) analyzed, still above 50 in each study. Precision is weaker than the headline 1190 suggests.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT-3.5, Marketing students scored higher on fluency (3.65 vs 2.52), originality (1.14 vs 0.79), and elaboration (1.50 vs 0.80), Management students higher on fluency (2.29 vs 1.78) and elaboration (1.99 vs 1.06) but not originality (p = .064), and Entrepreneurship students no different on any measure (Tables 1 and 2, PDF p. 10).
open_questions: The analyzed N per arm is not stated; the degrees of freedom imply about 202 (S1) and 122 (S2) of the 1190 recruited. Authors would need to supply arm-level n.
Tables 1 and 2 do not label the values in parentheses; their size relative to plausible arm sizes suggests standard errors rather than SDs, but the paper does not say.
How the three raters' scores were combined into one score per student (mean, sum, or other) is not stated.
Management 'Wilks Lambda = .07' with partial eta^2 = .33 looks internally inconsistent (Wilks of about .67 would match); the originality test is printed with df (1,198) instead of (1,120).

Should the paper's statement that 'Fluency serves as the primary index of creative ideation' (PDF p. 9) count as naming fluency the paper-primary outcome? I coded all outcomes as not_stated because the sentence justifies dropping flexibility rather than designating a primary outcome.
notes: One randomized trial split into two studies here because the two discipline groups did different tasks and were analyzed in separate MANOVAs; S1 and S2 come from one recruitment and some Management students were also in Marketing (duplicates removed, counts not stated). Design coded field_rct: the task ran in regular class sessions as a non-graded LMS item, administered by a researcher. The control arm could use internet search and other usual resources (coded ai_vs_bau). Pooled main effects in S1 come from the 2 x 2 MANOVA follow-up univariate tests; the paper reports Pillai's trace for the intervention main effect = 0.06, F(3, 196) = 4.63, p = .004, partial eta^2 = .06, and for S2 Wilks Lambda = .07, F(3, 118) = 19.92, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .33 (PDF p. 9-10). Text says the S1 pooled originality effect is significant but pooled fluency and elaboration are not, although Marketing shows large significant gains on both. Outlier removal followed non-normal residuals; Box's M was significant for the first MANOVA. No diversity or after-AI outcomes.
